title: Domes
hookLine: the dome as the heavens, with Christ Pantocrator looking down

cards: Over the center of some Orthodox churches, the ceiling doesn't stop. It curves up and closes into a dome, and from its very top a face looks down.
Christ, painted large, one hand raised in blessing, the other holding a book.
Around him, in some churches, angels circle; lower down, prophets and apostles; lower still, the walls with their saints; and at the bottom, the people, standing, heads tipped back.
Stand right under the center and the whole building seems to turn around that one face, the way the sky seems to turn around wherever you stand. Today: domes.

teach.h: A TENT STRETCHED OVER THE EARTH.
teach.b: A dome is a round roof. In an Orthodox church, it's also a picture of the sky. Isaiah describes God as the one "that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in."
A tent over the whole earth. A dome builds that tent over one congregation: a curved heaven, with everyone underneath at once.

teach.h: THE HEAVENS DECLARE THE GLORY OF GOD.
teach.b: Then, what the sky says: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." The psalm hears the real sky talking.
A painted dome makes it easier to hear: instead of clouds, faces, and the highest is Christ.
That image has a name: Christ Pantocrator. It's a Greek word from the New Testament itself.

In Revelation, the Lord says: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty." The Almighty, in the Greek, is pantokrator.
So the face at the top of the dome is the one Revelation calls the beginning and the end, blessing with one hand, holding the gospel book with the other. Last, the order of the room.

teach.h: IN EARTH, AS IT IS IN HEAVEN.
teach.b: Heaven at the top, earth at the bottom, and the walls between full of people who have lived on both. Orthodox Christians speak of the liturgy as heaven and earth worshiping together.
Under a dome, the Lord's Prayer can be heard almost as a description of the room: "Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." In that picture, heaven isn't far off up there.

how: In Orthodox churches built with a central dome, the dome is painted as the heavens, in some with Christ Pantocrator at its height, and worshipers stand beneath it during the Divine Liturgy.

o: a flat ceiling painted with scenes from Genesis
a tower built to hold a church's bells up high
a round roof painted as the heavens, Christ at the top

p: Isaiah: the sky as a tent
the glory of God, in the psalm

s: Pantocrator is a word that appears in the New Testament
in Revelation 1:8 the Greek pantokrator is rendered "the Almighty" in the King James.
an Orthodox dome is painted only to decorate the roof
it's a picture of the heavens, with Christ at the top and the people beneath.

games.q: you're painting the inside of a new dome. at its very top goes one image, seen from everywhere in the church. what goes there?
o: a starry sky with nothing in it
Christ, one hand blessing, the other holding a book
the names of everyone who built the church
games.why: in Orthodox churches the height of the dome is a place for Christ Pantocrator, the one Revelation calls the Almighty.

practice: Tip your head back gently and let your eyes find the center point of the ceiling above you, or of the sky if you're outside, and rest there. Then think of everyone under that same roof or sky right now.
If you pray, say the psalm's line, the heavens declare the glory of God, or simply stay under it, breathing.

wordCard.voice: Domes. In an Orthodox church, a round roof painted as the heavens, with Christ Pantocrator, the Almighty, looking down on everyone.

carryVoice: Your line: heaven overhead. One roof over everyone at once. Rest well.
